corpusSummary: Across 2026 social-science records, large language models are analyzed as interaction partners, research tools, and governance concerns across domains (HCI, health, education, environment, media). The corpus highlights trends in trust, embodiment, and user experience; LLMs as collaborative analytical instruments; equity and safety in health and policy contexts; education and learning analytics; and societal implications including polarization, culture, and public participation, all while noting methodological limitations and the need for validation and human oversight.

themes.name: Human–AI interaction, trust, embodiment, and social dynamics
themes.description: A range of studies examines perceived humanness vs. empathy, how richer AI presentations boost trust, how AI device embodiment affects well‑being and adoption, and how social networks and simulations reveal biases and polarization in AI‑mediated interactions.

themes.name: LLMs as research tools and methodological innovation
themes.description: Numerous works treat LLMs as analytical partners or workflow assistants for framing codebooks, sentiment analysis, data extraction, policy planning, and multi‑agent simulations, while calling for rigorous validation, transparency, and ethical oversight.

themes.name: Equity, safety, and governance in health, policy, and education
themes.description: Studies propose equity‑first governance in digital health, assess fairness in library/reference services, investigate health misinformation and safety/readability, and develop governance frameworks to address bias, cultural adequacy, and oversight.

themes.name: AI in education and learning analytics
themes.description: Research scrutinizes AI tutoring, game‑based learning, AI literacy among diverse learners, teacher competencies, and student engagement, alongside concerns about anxiety, overreliance, and pedagogical implications.

themes.name: Societal, cultural, and public‑participation implications of LLMs
themes.description: Evidence covers polarization, AI‑mediated religion and spirituality, heritage and urban planning, and public participation in decision‑making, highlighting both empowering possibilities and risks of misinformation, bias, and cultural insensitivity.
